source.title: Q-First: Most of Attention Needs Only the Query in Disaggregated LLM Decoding

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares model loss under altered sublayer orderings and query read points, using a different method from scaling-law sweeps. These results bear on V4, but it does not test scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations.
record.gate_note: The paper tests architecture/read-point changes and reports bits-per-byte loss outcomes at fixed parameter counts. It does not sweep model parameters, tokens, or compute to fit or extrapolate scaling laws. It does not test downstream predictability or other modalities.
record.test_reason: This is a systems paper on disaggregated decoding, not a scaling study. Section 7 trains 0.6B-parameter (596.05M) models from scratch on WikiText-103 at identical parameter count and forward arithmetic. It varies only sublayer order, attention read points or the parallel graph, and reports validation bits per byte. Those from-scratch results bear on V4, whether architecture details at fixed parameter count change loss only slightly. The conversion experiments (Section 6, Appendix B) measure the cost of rewiring an already-trained checkpoint, not the loss of an architecture trained as such. The authors say they are not a quality comparison between arrangements, so they do not bear on V4. No parameter, token or compute sweep is run, so V1–V3 and V5–V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but incomplete. The paper's main conclusion is that the cache-side device in disaggregated decoding needs only the query: the decomposition is exact, runs on stock kernels and returns a mergeable aggregate. On training, moving the query read point within Family A costs nothing measurable (at most 0.0011 bpb) at 3% of compute-optimal, where differences reflect disturbance to training rather than reachable quality. Reading queries from the network input costs +0.1003. A trained checkpoint can be converted by fine-tuning Wq alone, with a residual bounded above by +0.0142 (0.6B) and +0.0088 (4B). Deeper reads leave larger residuals. No speedup is measured.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not fit parameter-, token-, or compute-scaling curves. It varies sublayer ordering and query read points and evaluates bits-per-byte loss at reported fixed parameter counts.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported loss outcomes depend on read-point placement and block wiring; deeper read points and the shared network-input query differ from the one-half-layer and Family A settings. Family A differences are within the stated resolution, while the shared-query result is large. Seed variation matters for Shifted-Q.

fits_no_version.finding: Rewiring a trained checkpoint's query read point displaces loss: +0.0746 untrained at 0.6B and +0.0364 at 4B. Fine-tuning Wq leaves residuals of +0.0142 and +0.0088. The untrained displacement rises with read depth (+0.0658 to +0.4821 at 0.6B), and the post-repair residual rises with it (+0.0123 to +0.0556). A hybrid 27B model is displaced +0.0181 to +0.2081 forward-only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Post-hoc rewiring of trained transformers' attention read points costs loss that grows with read depth and shrinks with model scale, and is only partly recoverable by fine-tuning the query projection.

record.problems: The training comparison is one model family and scale on one corpus with 3 seeds, at three per cent of compute-optimal. The paper says these runs measure disturbance to training rather than reachable quality. Some comparisons have no reported uncertainty, and the fine-tuning result is described as an upper bound on residual conversion cost. No scaling-law fit is performed.
record.rows_left_out: No V4-relevant results were omitted. Per-arm held-out-test loss values are not reported; the paper gives only aggregate changes in gaps between validation and test splits.

untested.parts: No sweep of parameters, tokens or compute; no power-law fit.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.

No depth, width or aspect-ratio sweep. Only one scale (0.6B) and one corpus, at 3% of compute-optimal with a frozen embedding; whether the insensitivity persists at other scales or budgets is untested.
No other modalities or training regimes as power laws.
No fitting choices or exponents examined.

missing.what: Swapping sublayer order (feed-forward first) versus Standard at fixed parameters: every Family A arm sits −0.0623 to −0.0627 bpb below Standard. The authors attribute this to convergence rate and the frozen tied embedding and claim nothing from it. It is still a fixed-parameter architecture effect of about 5%, relevant to V4.
missing.locator: Section 7, 'The families are not compared across'

missing.what: Absolute validation loss of the Standard arm, and of Family B arms by seed (only differences are given except for Single-Q seeds).

Held-out test-split check: no gap moves between splits by more than 0.0094 across 18 arm-seeds, and by no more than 0.0020 in Family A. This guards the Family A null against selection on the validation split.
Family A arms separate above the seed band between roughly steps 1,000 and 5,000, and the separation is gone by the last third. Insensitivity depends on when training is evaluated.

record.verdict_notes: Relevance to scaling laws is indirect: the only bearing is on V4, through fixed-parameter-count architecture variants trained from scratch. The reader's T2 is changed to T3, since the study addresses a different question in a new setting. The conversion and forward-only rows are relinked to none because they measure perturbation or repair of trained weights, which the authors say is not an architecture quality comparison. The V4 evidence is one 0.6B model, one small corpus (WikiText-103, three epochs), a frozen tied embedding and 3 seeds at 3% of compute-optimal, so it is weak support. Qwen3.8-27B is the model name as given in the text.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law loss relationships in parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from smaller runs.
No systematic depth or width sweep, or broad survey of architecture families; tests concern sublayer order and query read-point variants in the reported models.
Other modalities and training regimes such as repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer as power-law settings.
Downstream-task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
Power-law fitting choices, exponents, compute-optimal splits, and whether scaling curves bend.
